summary: Describes EAP-TTLS version 0, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that wraps a TLS session. First the server, and optionally the client, is authenticated using TLS and keying material is made. Then a protected tunnel carries further information, such as legacy authentication, inside the tunnel. It is informational and later updated.

plainLanguage.summary: It first digs a secure tunnel using the same lock-and-key trick websites use, then passes the password through the tunnel so nobody can peek. It is used for joining Wi-Fi networks.

questions: what is the difference between eap-ttls and eap-tls
subtitle: A TLS tunnel for network login, so old password protocols can be used without exposing them to eavesdroppers.

tldr.problem: Legacy password protocols such as PAP, CHAP and MS-CHAP-V2 are exposed to dictionary attacks and eavesdropping on wireless links, yet there is a large installed base of password databases behind RADIUS and Diameter servers.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-TTLS first runs a TLS handshake that authenticates the server (and optionally the client), then tunnels the legacy authentication inside the TLS record layer as Diameter-style attribute-value pairs.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents what existing implementations do. It notes that the base version lacks cryptographic binding between outer and inner authentication, and it is updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9427.

today: RFC 5281 is an Informational RFC that is not obsoleted and is updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9427. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Password Logins
sections.content:
Most password protocols (CHAP, MS-CHAP, MS-CHAP-V2, EAP/MD5-Challenge) hash the password with a challenge. An eavesdropper who sees both challenge and response can run a dictionary attack, which works well because passwords usually have low entropy. Wired and dial-up users rarely worried about that. Wireless changes things: eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks are easier, usernames sent in the clear leak identity and location, and the access point may sit in an airport or hotel outside the user's provider.

The RFC lists what EAP-TTLS must deliver: support for legacy password protocols, passwords and identity hidden from observers, key material for the wireless data link, and support for roaming. It also states that EAP-TTLS is widely deployed and that this specification documents what existing implementations do.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting your secret word across a crowded room is risky. EAP-TTLS first puts you in a soundproof booth, then lets you say the secret word.

sections.title: Architecture and Layering
sections.content:
Four logical roles take part: the client, the access point, the TTLS server and the AAA/H server in the user's home domain. They may be combined in fewer boxes. The client and access point talk over a carrier such as PPP or EAPOL; the access point, TTLS server and AAA/H talk over RADIUS or Diameter. The AAA/H may be a legacy device that knows nothing about EAP-TTLS.

EAP-TTLS packets are carried in EAP, they encapsulate TLS, and TLS in turn carries attribute-value pairs (AVPs). When the inner login is itself EAP, an EAP method such as MD5-Challenge sits on top of the AVPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A visitor talks to a receptionist, who passes things to a security office, which checks the visitor against the company's old list. The old list never needs to learn any new tricks.

sections.title: The Two Phases
sections.content:
In phase 1 the TTLS server sends an EAP-TTLS/Start packet and a normal TLS handshake runs. It authenticates the server to the client and, optionally, the client to the server. Phase 1 ends when ChangeCipherSpec and Finished are exchanged. The RFC warns that if the null cipher suite is negotiated, there will be no security.

In phase 2 the TLS record layer tunnels AVPs between client and server. The TTLS server decrypts them and forwards any authentication data to the AAA/H, then relays challenges back. This continues until the AAA/H accepts or rejects the client.

Phase 2 is optional: it can be skipped after a successful session resumption or after client certificate authentication. For anonymity, the initial EAP-Response/Identity SHOULD NOT carry the real username; it SHOULD use a placeholder such as anonymous, optionally with a realm for routing.

TLS session resumption works as usual with session IDs, but tunneled authentication is not repeated for resumed sessions. A TTLS server MUST NOT permit a session to be resumed if the user was not successfully authenticated in phase 2. TLS 1.0, 1.1 or later MAY be used, and implementations SHOULD support TLS 1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: First the guard proves who he is and you both agree on a secret code. Then you prove who you are through the secret code. If you visited yesterday and remember the code, the guard may let you right in.

sections.title: Packets, Fragments and AVPs
sections.content:
An EAP-TTLS packet has Code (1 request, 2 response), Identifier, Length, Type, Flags, an optional four-octet Message Length and the Data. The EAP type is 21. The flags are L (length included), M (more fragments), S (start), two reserved bits and a version field V, set to 000 for EAP-TTLSv0.

Long messages are fragmented. Every fragment but the last has M set, the first fragment sets L and gives the total length, and the receiver of a packet with M set MUST send an Acknowledgement packet. Version negotiation happens in the first exchange: the server offers its highest version, and the client answers with the highest version it supports that is no higher.

Phase 2 data is encoded as AVPs in a format compatible with Diameter, though this does not mean Diameter must be supported. Each AVP in a Start packet must begin on a four-octet boundary and be zero-padded.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter is too big for the mailbox, it is cut into pieces and each piece is marked as number so-and-so. The receiver sends back a thumbs up for each piece.

sections.title: Keys and Inner Authentication Methods
sections.content:
After success, 128 octets of keying material are produced with the TLS PRF from the master secret, the constant string ttls keying material, and the client and server randoms. The first 64 octets are the MSK and the second 64 are the EMSK. The server hands this material to the access point over RADIUS or Diameter.

Challenge-based protocols such as CHAP and MS-CHAP normally use a challenge from the access point, which makes them open to replay. EAP-TTLS therefore derives the challenge itself from the TLS handshake using the string ttls challenge, so the client cannot choose it.

Inner methods include EAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP, MS-CHAP-V2 and PAP. Several inner authentications may run in turn, and success policy is up to client and server. Unless an application profile says otherwise, a compliant implementation MUST implement EAP as a tunneled method and MUST implement MD5-Challenge as an EAP type.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard and you both mix the same ingredients to cook up the same secret key. Nobody else has the ingredients, so nobody else can cook it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is open about a weakness: EAP-TTLSv0 lacks cryptographic binding between the TLS tunnel and the inner method. An attacker who poses as an authenticator to a legitimate client using an untunneled protocol could shuttle the credential proof into a tunneled one. Care should be taken not to use the same authentication protocol and credentials both inside the tunnel and outside it. An extension, [TTLS-EXT], was proposed to fix this, and users are strongly encouraged to adopt it.

Unlike many EAP methods, EAP-TTLS does not send the username in the clear in the first identity response, which supports anonymity. A party that receives a certificate in the handshake should validate the certification path to a trusted root. Version 0 is not subject to negotiating-down attacks, since it is the lowest version, but any higher version should define protection against them.
sections.plainLanguage: The booth is private, but you must check that the booth really belongs to the building. Otherwise a trickster might sit inside and listen.
